extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and readers/judges of poetry and drama (aspiring writers and literary critics)
extracted.subtask_short: writing and judging poetry and drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetry (especially heroic lyric and drama), emphasizing poetry's moral purpose, mnemonic/formal virtues, and dramatic rules (unity of time/place, in medias res, genre decorum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroical (epic) as the highest kind
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroical is 'not only a kind, but the best and most accomplished kind, of poetry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heroical poetry should set forth lofty images of worthies (e.g., Æneas, Achilles, Cyrus) that 'inflameth the mind with desire to be worthy' and 'inform with counsel how to be worthy.' Use exemplary actions across occasions (storms, war, peace, inward government) to present a complete model of virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as moral instruction and motivator
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry both 'teacheth and moveth to the most high and excellent truth' and is uniquely capable of teaching and moving toward virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose poetry so it instructs (comparable to philosophy/historiography in instruction) and moves (surpasses them in moving the reader). Use images and exempla to stir the reader from idleness to honourable enterprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as maker (creator of matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'only bringeth his own stuff, and doth not learn a conceit out of a matter, but maketh matter for a conceit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value imaginative invention: poets generate matters for thought rather than merely transcribe subjects. This creative agency is a defining strength and standard of poetic craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse (measure/rhyme) as a mnemonic and formal good
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse is 'the only fit speech for music' and 'far exceedeth prose in the knitting up of the memory.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer metrical form where memory and memorability are goals: measured words help retention because 'every word having his natural seat' and one word suggests the next. Verse is also suited to musical delivery and to condensing rules (grammar, logic, mathematics) into memorable lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry is not 'lying' because it does not affirm factual truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'nothing affirmeth, and therefore never lieth' — poetry presents what should or could be rather than asserting factual truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat poetry as imaginative representation (allegory, fiction). Use names and personae to enliven scenes without pretending historical assertion; the audience should be invited to understand figurative, not documentary, truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse of poetry does not condemn its right use
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if poetry is abused to corrupt, the abuse proves only that the thing abused can do great harm; rightly used it does the most good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetry by its proper use and effects (does it teach goodness and delight?) rather than by the uses to which ill-disposed authors may put it. Compare other arts (physic, law, scripture) which when abused cause harm but are valuable when rightly used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three supports for poetic genius: art, imitation, exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's genius must be guided by three wings: 'art, imitation, and exercise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage study of art (rules/technique), imitation of good models, and disciplined practice. Genius alone is insufficient; craft and learned imitation improve and direct natural talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orderly matter and well-chosen words (marshal matter into assured rank)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic matter must not be 'quodlibet' (anything at random); poets should not 'never marshalling it into any assured rank.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange material with deliberate structure so the reader can follow progression. Avoid a sequence of verses that merely beget each other without an ordering principle; ensure coherence between content and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exemplary narratives in full variety of circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: A good heroic picture shows the exemplar 'how in storms, how in sports, how in war, how in peace, how a fugitive, how victorious, how besieged, how besieging...inward self...outward government.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building exemplars (heroes), present them in a range of situations to teach different virtues and practical counsel; variety strengthens the exemplar's instructional capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama: unity of place
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage should 'always represent but one place.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid abrupt shifts of scene that force actors to announce their location. Keep the physical setting coherent so the audience understands the represented space without contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama: unity of time
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'uttermost time presupposed' should be short (Aristotle's precept): a tragedy should not span many days or years unrealistically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compress action into a plausible chronological window (classically 'one day' or a tightly bounded period) to preserve dramatic plausibility; avoid telescoping decades into a two-hour performance unless conventional devices justify it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin in medias res (not ab ovo)
rubrics_metrics.description: A play should 'not... begin “ab ovo,” but... come to the principal point of that one action which they will represent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open at the decisive moment rather than with long backstory; present prior events by report or clever devices (e.g., a messenger) rather than staging lengthy antecedent scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate reporting from representing
rubrics_metrics.description: Some things 'may be told, which cannot be showed' — drama must recognize limits of representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose to narrate events that are impractical to stage (shipwrecks, distant lands) and represent only what can be credibly enacted. Use messengers or chorus to report off-stage action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing high tragedy with low clownishness (genre decorum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays should not 'mingl[e] kings and clowns... thrust in the clown by head and shoulders to play a part in majestical matters'—avoid mongrel tragi-comedy without cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep tonal register appropriate: do not insert coarse buffoonery into lofty scenes where it undermines admiration and commiseration. If mixing occurs, do so only with clear artistic justification and classical precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: delight precedes laughter; structure matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians 'think there is no delight without laughter, which is very wrong; for though laughter may come with delight, yet cometh it not of delight.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write comedy to produce structured delight (wit, situation, moral balance) rather than pursuing crude laughter alone. Aim for a sustained comic design rather than episodic jests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain decency and avoid scurrility in public performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Many plays contain 'scurrility, unworthy of any chaste ears' or 'extreme show of doltishness' that detracts from art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard public performances against indecent or vulgar elements that offend decorum; ensure the comic or clown parts serve the whole and respect audience sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ancient models as instructive exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite and learn from ancients: Homer, Pindar, Virgil, Theocritus, et al., who furnish patterns and high examples for poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitate the virtues of classical models (structure, moral force, measured diction) while adapting them to contemporary language and needs; study their handling of scene, memory, and moral exempla.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names in fiction are theatrical devices, not assertions of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving names ('Cyrus' 'Æneas') is to 'make their picture the more lively' and 'not to build any history.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feel free to name invented characters to vivify representation; naming does not convert fiction into false historical assertion but aids dramatic vividness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should be fit for music and oral delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse is praised as 'the only fit speech for music—the most divine striker of the senses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing for song or recitation, prioritize rhythmic and sonic qualities that enhance musical performance and sensorial impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's social/educative function: suitable for public instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is used in Holy Scripture and by Christ; it 'teacheth goodness, and delight the learners of it' and has been used to compile rules for many arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider poetry's pedagogical capacity: craft verse that can instruct communities, transmit moral precepts, and serve as a public vehicle of good example.
